power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Rhythm as a prism into predictive coding in autism

text.text: We propose rhythm cognition, the perception of and engagement with patterns of stimuli organized in time, as a prism for investigating predictive coding in autism.

Predictive coding theories of autism are common, driven by the prevalence of predictive coding in contemporary cognitive models and their efficacy relating autism to other neuropsychiatric conditions.
However, different theories manifest in similar behavior, making them difficult to compare, and rely on an over-encompassing, domain-general conceptualization of predictive coding itself.
Here, we conduct a narrative review demonstrating how computational models of rhythm processing enable precise, highly individualized characterizations of predictive coding theories of autism.

To do this, we synergize behavioral and neuroscientific scholarship on rhythm processing in autistic and nonautistic individuals with research probing developmental trajectories of beat and meter induction.
We then discuss several canonical models of rhythm processing, detailing the strengths and shortcomings of mapping each model onto specific manifestations of predictive coding in autism.
We conclude that rhythm processing can reveal individualized differences in predictive coding mechanisms in autism, moving beyond a categorical, subtypefocused view of cognitive mechanisms in autism.
Autism is a common (1 in 31 [1]) neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences or impairments in social function and restricted interests or repetitive behaviors [2].

text.text: Autistic individuals are quite heterogeneous in presentation, leading some scholars to advocate for considering a plurality of autisms, rather than one singular condition [3] [4] [5].

text.text: Since any presentation can be driven by several underlying cognitive mechanisms, a plethora of mechanistic theories of autism have emerged over the last several decades.
While such theories share common characteristics, they often operate from entirely different perspectives.

Some theories are based on a cognitive perspective, whether characterizing differences in cognitive processes like mentalizing [6, 7], or comparing reliance on cognitive styles such as systemizing over empathizing [8, 9] or deliberative over intuitive [10].

text.text: Because of this, predictive coding theories of autism provide a cognitively grounded, neurologically instantiated explanatory mechanism for autism that integrates well within a broader transdiagnostic framework.
These properties make predictive coding particularly attractive as our understanding of the co-occurrence of autism and other conditions expands.

Particularly in light of potential pitfalls of characterizing cognitive mechanisms as either domain-specific or domain-general [45], it is imperative to derive generalizations from mechanistic theory linking observed domains, rather than relying on the assumption that there exists one predictive network that is used, in its entirety, across all contexts and tasks.

text.text: We argue that it enables us to examine detailed, nuanced aspects of inference-making, mechanistically linked to autistic traits and behavior, in ways that are both applicable to a wide range of cognitive domains and highly sensitive to small variations in cognitive processing.

Our definition of rhythm distinguishes it from timing, which includes phenomena such as interval discrimination that do not involve making inferences about patterns, but is historically the most common approach used to study temporal processing in autism [46].

text.text: We review approaches to studying rhythm, connect rhythm with aspects of the autism phenotype, and establish rhythm's relevance for building theories of autism.

Then, we detail how modern advances in computational models of rhythm perception and temporal prediction may be applied to study differences in predictive coding in autism, including potential pitfalls of such an approach.
This implies that rhythm functions as a prism into predictive coding, with a particular utility in probing prediction mechanisms implicated in autism.

Rhythm is uniquely suited to disambiguating predictive coding theories of autism, because different predictive coding theories manifest differently in rhythm processing tasks, and because rhythm is a core component of several autistic traits.

In short, rhythmic processing acts as a prism, splitting the "white light" of behavior, which is the end product of a wide range of possible cognitive and mechanistic components, into its constituent parts.

Rhythm tasks are particularly useful because they are highly applicable beyond the experimental task itself; informative at every developmental stage from early infancy through late adulthood; and are well-framed in testable, computational terms.

text.text: They can be separated along three dimensions: construct of interest, observation modality (e.g. behavioral vs. neural), and active vs. passive.
Behavioral tasks tend to be active, while neural tasks tend to be passive, although there are exceptions to this rule.

Excluding research on time estimation, which does not meet our definition of rhythm processing, most behavioral research in autism has focused on two constructs: synchronization, or the ability to align with an isochronous stimulus; and differentiation, or the ability to tell whether two rhythms are the same and correctly aligned.
Neural research focuses primarily on synchronization and oddball detection, both in autism and in neurotypical populations.
In recent years, novel paradigms using musical rhythm to uncover autism-related changes in predictive coding have emerged.
For instance, a recent study by Vishne et al. tested how autistic and nonautistic participants corrected their tapping in response to periodic changes in the speed of an auditory stimulus [32].
text.formatted: For instance, a recent study by Vishne et al. tested how autistic and nonautistic participants corrected their tapping in response to periodic changes in the speed of an auditory stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Another study by Cannon et al. used a combination of synchronization, stimulus detection (detecting unrelated stimuli at different points in an ongoing rhythmic cycle), continuation (tapping at the same pace as a stimulus after the stimulus has ended), and adaptation (updating a tapping rate to match changes in a stimulus) to demonstrate increased sensory noise among autistic participants [40].

text.text: Passive behavioral tasks are particularly promising in probing temporal prediction in autism: while visual attention to a singer's eyes synchronizes to the beat of the song they are singing as early as infancy [56], autistic toddlers' visual attention adapts to temporally unpredictable stimuli consistent with a slowly-updating rhythmic prior [34].

text.text: While neural approaches to studying several constructs, most notably synchronization, oddball or stimulus detection, and adaptation, are well-established, they are not applied in autism as frequently as with nonautistic populations.

However, since the neurological evidence dovetails with behavioral correlates in nonautistic participants, they could provide similarly informative results when investigating autism-related changes in patterns of neural activity.

As a result, studying the neural correlates of temporal prediction and rhythm processing in autism is an extremely powerful, yet underutilized, tool for probing nuanced variation in predictive coding in autism.
Different rhythm tasks also evince different patterns of performance in autism, which can be mapped onto predictive coding processes.

For instance, Vishne et al. used changes in the tempo of an ongoing stimulus to demonstrate that autistic individuals did not update their inferred tempo as quickly or accurately as nonautistic peers [32], while Cannon et al. found that autistic participants adjusted to temporal offsets similarly to nonautistic peers, although they did show evidence of a less precise internal timing mechanism in autism [40].

text.text: These tasks are similar, since they both contend with error correction, but while Vishne et al. investigated changes in tempo (i.e. how fast stimuli are happening), Cannon et al. investigated changes in phase (i.e. location in a rhythmic cycle).

While these results may at first appear contradictory, they may be collectively explained by a nuanced view of predictive coding that allows for heterogeneity across individuals and separability of different components or parameters of predictive coding itself.
This task-specificity means that rhythm tasks can reveal predictive processing in autism with unprecedented detail and precision.
Notably, and in contrast to older research, these recent studies leverage rhythmic perturbations, or moments where a predictable rhythm is defied.
Such perturbations may be necessary for revealing nuanced differences in rhythm processing mechanisms, since each model behaves similarly when the stimulus is highly predictable.
Put simply, if the task is too easy, every model or participant looks the same.
Harnessing rhythmic complexity or unpredictability increases rhythm's usefulness as a prism into underlying mechanisms in autism.
Rhythm processing's utility for probing predictive coding in autism rests on two key properties.

First, while no single mechanism addresses all aspects of cognition, and no single measurement modality can capture variation in every characteristic of autism, rhythm is central to a remarkably broad range of autistic traits, ranging from fluid social interaction and communication to motor impairments.
This considerable overlap between rhythm processing and autism's heterogeneous presentation greatly enhances its direct applicability.
Second, rhythm processing is not constant over an individual's life.
Instead, it changes in response to maturing sensory processing, enculturation and statistical learning, and overall patterns of neurodevelopment.

It is also relevant at every age; beat induction, for example, has been observed even in perinatal populations, and rhythm scaffolds (visual) attention patterns in infants as young as 2 months, limited mostly by the postnatal development of the visual system [78].

text.text: Children also demonstrate a rapidly maturing capacity to infer abstract patterns from rhythms and use those patterns to scaffold attention and behavior.
In particular, they learn to recognize and rely on hierarchical rhythmic structures, or meters, where some beats are stronger than others.

text.text: Meter perception is, therefore, the outcome of a complex learning and classification process that applies top-down predictive processing to help navigate a temporally complex sensory environment.
Unlike beat induction, which matures with sensory and motor functionality, meter induction evolves with exposure, enculturation, learning, and the development of classification abilities.

Taken together, these findings imply two distinct contributors to rhythm processing: bottom-up beat entrainment, which develops as sensory and motor skills mature; and top-down metric inference, which relies on learning and classification mechanisms [90].

text.text: The earliest example of a rhythmic theory dynamically incorporating prediction error is Wing and Kristofferson's linear error-correction model [153].
text.formatted: The earliest example of a rhythmic theory dynamically incorporating prediction error is Wing and Kristofferson's linear error-correction model <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">[153]</ref>.

text.text: Their framework represents someone tapping a constant beat as an internal timekeeper that triggers a motor response at regular intervals.

It has two potential sources of noise: variance in the intervals measured out by the timekeeper, and variance in the motor delay between the timekeeper triggering a pulse and the person producing a tap.

Given a sequence of taps, this model decomposes variance in the inter-tap interval into estimates of timekeeper noise and motor noise, which in turn determine the linear coefficient by which tap onset error is corrected.
In a predictive coding context, this linear error-correction model substitutes for an internal model of the rhythmgenerating process, or a temporal theory of mind.
Under this analogy, variance of the temporal timekeeper corresponds to stability of the rhythmic prior, while variance of the response delay corresponds to sensory noise.

Since this approach explicitly couches rhythm perception as an internal cognitive model of an external process, it capitalizes on established links between predictive coding and mentalizing, which is known to be altered in autism.
While this mapping is very clean, making this model very interpretable, it has several key limitations.
First, it assumes that the error correction is linear, so an error of a given size will always result in the exact same correction.
Second, it assumes that the error correction is constant, rather than learned and adapted over time.
Third, it is only specified for isochronous beats, and does not generalize easily to more complex rhythmic structures.
Last, although it is simple enough to be interpretable and easily solved, it is underspecified compared to more recent models of timing.

While it is a useful starting point for this kind of analysis, since it demonstrates how models of rhythm perception can map onto broader theories of cognition, newer models will provide more opportunities to study rhythm processing.
These models largely fall into two categories: top-down probabilistic models, usually employing Bayesian mathematics; and bottom-up neurodynamic models.

Cannon's phase inference through point process estimation (PIPPET) model [154] and its extension to simultaneous inference of cyclic phase and tempo [155] represents a more nuanced approach to temporal prediction.
text.formatted: Cannon's phase inference through point process estimation (PIPPET) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">[154]</ref> and its extension to simultaneous inference of cyclic phase and tempo <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">[155]</ref> represents a more nuanced approach to temporal prediction.

text.text: Unlike the linear error-correction model, this class of model relies on continuous Bayesian inference.

In its most complete manifestation, this approach models rhythms as a system of differential equations where the probability of an onset is a function of phase (metric template), phase changes at a rate determined by tempo (the derivative of phase is a function of tempo), and both phase and tempo are sampled from some prior distribution.
At each time step, the presence or absence of an onset is observed and compared against the expectation, and that error updates the probability distributions over phase and tempo.
This model is governed by several key parameters, which may admit a few kinds of cognitive interpretations.

Uncertainty over both tempo and phase reflect the strength of a prior distribution, in conjunction with the ratio governing whether error is ascribed primarily to phase misalignment or incorrect tempo specification.

The specificity of the metric template also is a form of prior, as is the tempo correction coefficient governing how strongly a listener returns to their preferred tempo in the absence of reinforcement.
Together, this presents a much more realistic rhythmic prior than Wing and Kristofferson's timekeeper.
Sensory noise, like in the linear error-correction model, manifests as a single parameter.
Such a parametrization within a Bayesian context enables precise mappings between model parameters and theorized cognitive or perceptual parameters.
In theory, the complexity of the rhythmic prior enables an extraordinary degree of nuance for a cognitive model of rhythm processing.
However, it is constrained in two key ways.
The detailed specification of the model means it can be difficult, in practice, to distinguish between behaviors driven by certain parameters.
In addition, as a top-down model, it is difficult to connect specific parameters to underlying neurological correlates.
These limitations are not necessarily fatal for use of the PIPPET family of models in fitting predictive coding parameters to rhythmic prediction.
The difficulty specifying which parameters drive observed changes in behavior or neural activity may be resolved by simplifying the parameter space itself.

For instance, uncertainty over tempo, uncertainty over phase, and the ratio governing how learning is distributed across tempo and phase could all be combined into two parameters, one specifying overall uncertainty and the other distributing that uncertainty between phase and tempo.
Using places where changes in parameters result in strongly connected shifts in predicted behavior as a basis to simplify the PIPPET model could improve its empirical applicability.
The absence of neural correlates, meanwhile, is counteracted by the nature of PIPPET's outputs.

At each time step, the model generates expectations for tempo, phase, and the likelihood of an onset, along with a measure of the surprisal generated by comparing the last of these expectations against an observation.

Each of these output measures does map onto an observable feature of standard neuroelectric imaging such as magneto/encephalography (M/EEG): expected tempo relates to frequency tagging, beta-band oscillatory power maps onto expected phase, and surprisal is indexed by the mismatch field event-related potential.
As a result, the lack of direct identifiability between model parameters and neural substrates is secondary to model-fitting, a property typical of probabilistic cognitive models in general.
Predictive coding theories of autism generally involve shifts in one of two sets of parameters: the specificity of a perceptual prior, or the precision of a perceived error.
The PIPPET family of models includes priors over phase, tempo, and pattern of onsets, so changing the uncertainty over any of these alters the specificity of the prior.
These changes can be global, implying uniformly weaker or stronger priors, or parameter-specific, although this may be constrained by limited identifiability.

Error precision is not implemented as directly in PIPPET, but can be manipulated by changing the background probability of an onset not driven by the rhythmic pattern, since a higher such probability leads to integrating errors more hesitantly.
Changing the uncertainty over observation timing (i.e. sensory noise) would also impact how readily errors were integrated into the model.

The key difference between these two mechanisms of changing error precision is the source of uncertainty: the probability of a non-rhythmic event represents error from outside the perceiver, while sensory noise is error from inside.
Neural resonance theory is perhaps the most neurologically grounded rhythmic synchronization theory.
It builds on coupled populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons with simple differential equations governing how their activity dynamically interacts.
First described by Wilson and Cowan [158], these coupled neural populations behave like driven damped oscillators given a regular sensory input.
text.formatted: First described by Wilson and Cowan <ref type="bibr" target="#b158">[158]</ref>, these coupled neural populations behave like driven damped oscillators given a regular sensory input.

text.text: These excitatory and inhibitory neural populations map very cleanly onto the "canonical microcircuit" view of predictive coding [159].
text.formatted: These excitatory and inhibitory neural populations map very cleanly onto the "canonical microcircuit" view of predictive coding <ref type="bibr" target="#b159">[159]</ref>.

text.text: Sensory input arrives at the internal granular layer, where prediction errors are encoded, and then propagated in two streams: an excitatory stream making inferences about the hidden schema driving the observations, and an inhibitory stream making inferences about the (also hidden) state of the rhythmic process.
This resembles a neural oscillator, albeit much more complex than a classical Wilson-Cowan manifestation.
The neural resonance approach can, with some modifications, also integrate with a more recent neuroanatomical theory called predictive routing [160].
text.formatted: The neural resonance approach can, with some modifications, also integrate with a more recent neuroanatomical theory called predictive routing <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">[160]</ref>.

text.text: Unlike the proposed neural predictive coding microcircuit, which proposes that predictions and associated errors are encoded by neuron-level spiking activity, predictive routing characterizes prediction and error integration via oscillatory activity in neural populations Low-frequency oscillations propagate from higher cortical areas (i.e. prefrontal cortex) to sensory regions, while high-frequency oscillations go the opposite direction.

Since low-frequency oscillations inhibit high-frequency activity at certain phases (e.g. delta-beta phase locking), while high-frequency activity is enhanced by sensory input, predictive routing takes on the same classic inhibitory-excitatory oscillator structure as well.
This structure could explain canonical patterns like shifts in beta and gamma oscillatory power associated with the beat frequency [60], which the classic predictive coding version does not.
text.formatted: This structure could explain canonical patterns like shifts in beta and gamma oscillatory power associated with the beat frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref>, which the classic predictive coding version does not.

text.text: Although this model is based on excitatory and inhibitory neural activity, it incorporates several simplifications that are not neurobiologically justified.
It assumes all connections are instantaneous, rather than incorporating time delays associated with signal transmission through axons, myelinated or otherwise.
In addition, it does not integrate any structural hypothesis of where rhythm sits in the brain, instead relying on generic neural populations.

On a less neuroanatomical level, these oscillator models assume that the broader neural context surrounding the excitatory and inhibitory populations is static; essentially, this assumption means that nothing outside rhythm processing affects rhythm processing.
Unlike PIPPET, the internal parameters of a neural resonance model can, in theory, be fit to observable neurological data.

In addition, although a simple Wilson-Cowan oscillator alone cannot account for complex rhythm structures or microtiming variation, more complex collections of oscillators are sensitive to such phenomena [161].
text.formatted: In addition, although a simple Wilson-Cowan oscillator alone cannot account for complex rhythm structures or microtiming variation, more complex collections of oscillators are sensitive to such phenomena <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">[161]</ref>.

text.text: Under the canonical view of predictive coding, where predictions propagate as inhibitory activity from higher to lower cortical layers or brain regions and errors return as excitatory activity the other direction, error precision is easily parametrized as the connection from excitatory to inhibitory populations within the oscillator.
The strength of the sensory prior would, in a naive sense, be the complementary inhibitory connection.
This implies that all predictive coding theories of autism may be simply instantiated by increasing or decreasing one of those parameters.
Furthermore, the Wilson-Cowan excitatory-inhibitory loop is only one instantiation of a driven or forced oscillator.

In general terms, such oscillators are defined in terms of a natural frequency and damping coefficient, each of which may include (relatively small) variation in time; introducing both random variation to these parameters can approximate the uncertainty typical in a predictive coding framework.
Taking such a tactic allows neural resonance models to represent predictive coding theories of autism in very nuanced ways.
Neural resonance's focus on oscillatory dynamics situates neural resonance squarely in a dynamical systems framework, where making predictions is largely unnecessary [162].
text.formatted: Neural resonance's focus on oscillatory dynamics situates neural resonance squarely in a dynamical systems framework, where making predictions is largely unnecessary <ref type="bibr" target="#b162">[162]</ref>.

text.text: However, since an oscillatory model can be modified to represent predictive coding theories of autism, it is ideally suited for bridging predictive coding and neurobiological modelling architectures.
We have proposed rhythm processing as a prism through which we can probe predictive coding mechanisms of autism.

This approach is in line with recent proposals for a temporal science of behavior [163] and arguments that temporal prediction is a useful bridge between music and language perception in autism [164], making it both relevant and timely for current directions in the field.
text.formatted: This approach is in line with recent proposals for a temporal science of behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">[163]</ref> and arguments that temporal prediction is a useful bridge between music and language perception in autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">[164]</ref>, making it both relevant and timely for current directions in the field.

text.text: Furthermore, temporal prediction capitalizes on existing techniques to test theories of autism, rather than requiring the invention of novel measurement approaches.

This immediacy makes temporal prediction particularly suited to filling the urgent need for deeper understanding of how autism works in practice, rather than just in theory, while also providing a solid foundation for further methodological development and innovation.

It also allows for increased sensitivity to individual differences and task characteristics, which in turn allows researchers to parse which theories are applicable for which people, and in which contexts.
Given rhythm's applicability to a wide range of autism symptoms, such specificity is of particular use in translational scenarios, where empirical results are used for clinical applications.
